stem: According to the theory of plate tectonics, the Himalayas were formed by the collision of the Indian plate with the:
solution: The Himalayas formed when the northward-moving Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate, folding the sediments of the Tethys Sea.

stem: The sea that existed between the Indian plate and the Eurasian plate before the Himalayas formed was the:
solution: The Tethys Sea's sediments were folded up to form the Himalayas as the plates collided.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the major physiographic divisions of India?
solution: India's physiographic divisions are the Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains and Islands. The Sahara is in Africa.

stem: The Himalayas are divided longitudinally into how many parallel ranges?
solution: The Himalayas consist of three parallel ranges: the Himadri (Great Himalayas), the Himachal (Middle Himalayas) and the Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas).

stem: The northernmost and highest range of the Himalayas, containing the loftiest peaks, is the:
solution: The Himadri (Great Himalayas) is the northernmost, highest and most continuous range, containing peaks like Everest and Kanchenjunga.

stem: The outermost range of the Himalayas is the:
solution: The Shiwaliks form the outermost (southernmost) range of the Himalayas.

stem: The longitudinal valleys lying between the Shiwaliks and the Himachal (Middle Himalayas) are called:
solution: The valleys between the Shiwaliks and the Middle Himalayas are called 'Duns' (e.g. Dehra Dun).

stem: The highest peak located within India is:
solution: Kanchenjunga is the highest peak in India (Mount Everest lies in Nepal).

stem: The Middle Himalayas contain famous ranges such as the Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar and:
solution: The Himachal (Middle Himalayas) includes the Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar and Mahabharat ranges.

stem: The Northern Plains of India were formed by the deposition of alluvium by three river systems: the Indus, the Ganga and the:
solution: The Northern Plains were built up by alluvium deposited by the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra and their tributaries.

stem: The narrow belt of pebbles and rocks deposited at the foothills where rivers emerge from the mountains is called the:
solution: The Bhabar is a narrow belt of pebble deposits along the foothills where streams deposit their load and disappear underground.

stem: The wet, marshy region south of the Bhabar, where streams re-emerge, is called the:
solution: South of the Bhabar lies the Terai — a wet, marshy and forested belt where the underground streams reappear.

stem: The new, younger alluvium of the floodplains, renewed almost every year, is called:
solution: Khadar is the newer alluvium, deposited by floods each year, making the floodplains fertile.

stem: The older alluvium of the plains, which lies above the floodplains, is called:
solution: Bhangar is the older alluvium, forming terraces above the floodplains, often containing calcareous deposits (kankar).

stem: The Peninsular Plateau is divided into the Central Highlands and the:
solution: The Peninsular Plateau consists of the Central Highlands (north of the Narmada) and the Deccan Plateau (south of the Narmada).

stem: The Central Highlands lie to the north of which river?
solution: The Central Highlands lie north of the Narmada river, bounded by the Vindhyan and Aravali ranges.

stem: The Western Ghats are also known as the:
solution: The Western Ghats are also called the Sahyadris.

stem: Compared with the Eastern Ghats, the Western Ghats are:
solution: The Western Ghats are higher and more continuous, whereas the Eastern Ghats are lower and discontinuous (dissected by rivers).

stem: The highest peak of the Western Ghats and of peninsular (South) India is:
solution: Anai Mudi is the highest peak of the Western Ghats and of peninsular India.

stem: The black soil (regur), ideal for cotton, found on the Deccan Plateau is formed from:
solution: The black soil of the Deccan is derived from the basaltic lava of the Deccan Trap volcanic rocks.

stem: The Indian (Thar) Desert lies mainly in which state?
solution: The Indian Desert (Thar) lies mainly in Rajasthan, to the west of the Aravali hills.

stem: The only large river of the Thar Desert region is the:
solution: The Luni is the only significant river of the arid Thar Desert region.

stem: The coastal plain on the western side of the peninsula includes the Konkan, Kannad and:
solution: The western coastal plain comprises the Konkan (north), the Kannad plain (central) and the Malabar coast (south).

stem: The eastern coastal plain in its southern part is known as the:
solution: The southern part of the eastern coastal plain is called the Coromandel coast; the northern part is the Northern Circars.

stem: The Lakshadweep Islands are composed of:
solution: The Lakshadweep Islands are coral islands, made of coral deposits.

stem: The only active volcano in India is located on which island?
solution: Barren Island in the Andaman and Nicobar group is home to India's only active volcano.

stem: The eastern extension of the Himalayas, bending sharply to the south along the eastern boundary, forms the:
solution: The Purvanchal hills are the eastern extension of the Himalayas along India's north-eastern boundary.

stem: The Peninsular Plateau is one of the __________ landmasses of the Earth.
solution: The Peninsular Plateau is part of the ancient Gondwana land and is one of the oldest and most stable landmasses on Earth.

stem: The Northern Plains are important because they are:
options: Very fertile and densely populated, supporting intensive agriculture
solution: The alluvial Northern Plains are highly fertile and densely populated, supporting intensive agriculture.

stem: The Aravali range, one of the oldest fold mountains, runs across which region?
solution: The Aravali Range, among the world's oldest fold mountains, runs across Rajasthan in north-western India.

stem: The Vindhya and Satpura ranges are located in the:
solution: The Vindhya and Satpura ranges are part of the Peninsular Plateau, forming the boundary of the Central Highlands and the Deccan.

stem: The gaps (passes) in the Western Ghats that allow movement include the Thal, Bhor and:
solution: The Western Ghats have passes like the Thal, Bhor and Pal Ghat that allow movement across them.

stem: The Deccan Plateau is a triangular landmass bordered by the __________ Ghats on both sides.
solution: The Deccan Plateau is bordered by the Western Ghats on the west and the Eastern Ghats on the east.

stem: The Himalayas act as a climatic barrier by:
options: Blocking cold winds from Central Asia and trapping monsoon winds
solution: The Himalayas block the cold, dry winds of Central Asia and force the monsoon winds to shed rain, greatly influencing India's climate.

stem: Which physiographic division is known as the 'roof of the world' region and the source of major rivers?
solution: The Himalayan Mountains are a great source of perennial rivers, fed by their snow and glaciers.

stem: The rivers Narmada and Tapi flow through which type of valley in the Peninsular Plateau?
solution: The Narmada and Tapi flow through rift valleys (trough faults) in the Peninsular Plateau, flowing westwards.

stem: The Deccan Trap region is famous for its:
options: Black soil formed from volcanic basalt
solution: The Deccan Trap, formed from ancient volcanic (basaltic) eruptions, gives rise to the fertile black cotton soil.

stem: The Western Coastal Plains are narrow, while the Eastern Coastal Plains are:
options: Broad and level with large deltas
solution: The Eastern Coastal Plains are broad and level, formed by the large deltas of rivers like the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.

stem: The islands in the Bay of Bengal (Andaman and Nicobar) are believed to be:
options: The elevated portions of submarine mountains
solution: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are thought to be the elevated portions of submarine mountains.

stem: Which of the following pairs (range — location) is correctly matched?
solution: The Aravali is in Rajasthan. The Sahyadris are the Western Ghats, the Purvanchal is in the North-East, and the Vindhyas are in the Peninsular Plateau.

stem: The physical diversity of India is important because it:
options: Provides varied resources — minerals, forests, fertile land and water
solution: India's varied physiography provides a wide range of resources — minerals, forests, fertile plains, water and more.

stem: The Great Himalayas are also called the:
solution: The Great (Inner) Himalayas are also called the Himadri.

stem: The Chota Nagpur Plateau, rich in minerals, is a part of the:
solution: The Chota Nagpur Plateau, known for its mineral wealth, is part of the Peninsular Plateau.

stem: The northern plains are broadly divided into the Punjab plains, the Ganga plains and the:
solution: The Northern Plains are divided into the Punjab Plains (west), the Ganga Plains (centre) and the Brahmaputra Plains (east).

stem: The high mountains of the Himalayas are a source of great rivers because they:
options: Store water as snow and glaciers, feeding perennial rivers
solution: The Himalayan snow and glaciers feed perennial rivers like the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra throughout the year.

stem: The Deccan Plateau slopes generally towards the:
options: East (so most peninsular rivers flow eastwards)
solution: The Deccan Plateau generally slopes from west to east, which is why most large peninsular rivers flow eastwards into the Bay of Bengal.

stem: The coastal plains are important for:
solution: The coastal plains support agriculture, fishing, salt-making, ports and maritime trade.

stem: The Indian desert has features such as:
solution: The Thar Desert has features like crescent-shaped sand dunes (barchans) and receives very low rainfall.

stem: The Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats meet at which hills in the south?
solution: The Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats meet at the Nilgiri Hills in southern India.

stem: The overall theme of 'Physical Features of India' is that:
options: India has diverse physiographic divisions formed by different geological processes
solution: The chapter explains India's diverse physiographic divisions — mountains, plains, plateau, desert, coasts and islands — formed by different geological processes.
